doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Wanting to film Clifford Brown
summary: Crohn would like to film Clifford Brown, a clean-living trumpeter who died in a car accident, unlike many other trumpeters.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Are there jazz people out there now that you would like to focus on with a film, or a group of them?

I think the last time I really was moved and wanted to do a film about a jazz person image was Clifford Brown. And that was twenty years ago. I really wanted to do that film, because I loved Clifford’s playing. And who he was as a man. He ran sort of counter to the prevailing jazz of the fifties, which was people who were debauched, they did heroin and you’d see people playing and nodding off while they’re playing. And he was a mathematician, he was a chess player, he was a clean liver, he was a beautiful, sweet soul, and he died not of an overdose. I mean there’s a history of trumpet players dying young. Bix Beiderbecke from drink; Bunny Berigan from drink.

Fats Navarro from drugs. Lee Morgan from being killed on the bandstand. I mean, and in the face of all that, there’s Clifford you know, full of life, cut down by a car accident. So I want to capture that goodness on film. I really want to make a film about Clifford and shoot in places where he played and interview the people who knew him. That’s the last film I really had a love in my heart to do. I do with Sangeeta but he just was presented to me. I didn’t know who Sangeeta was. So I have more call to do films now on healers and shamans and spiritual people. Or not do films at all. I mean, you know, it’s time to move on and do something else. Somebody asked me about — I said the only thing worse about the film I’m making on Sangeeta, because it’s been very hard, making this film on Sangeeta, is not making this film on Sangeeta. Because I really do love him and making the film, it’s just very hard. And I don’t know what I’d be doing if I weren’t doing it. We’ve certainly gone all over the place, haven’t we?
We have indeed. That’s what I like about interviews. You never know where you’re going to go with it.
